sheet would agree ~100%, so each is genuine evidence. Neither is official; UPSC
publishes no key for this sitting and none is expected.

Centurion vs Dreamers  135  90.0%

OUR BLIND PASS SITS CLOSER TO CENTURION THAN THE TWO KEYS SIT TO EACH OTHER.
That does not make our derivation authoritative, but it does retire the framing
of the first adjudication, which treated a lone key as the external signal and
deferred to it on every recall row. With two keys the deference rule needs a
majority to defer TO, and on 10 of the 16 original disagreements there is none.
THE ADJUDICATION AXIS IS DERIVABLE-vs-RECALL, NOT PART A vs PART B.
DERIVABLE — Part A, plus any Part B item settled by science, a textbook
statement, or the stem's own words. The derivation wins where it is
decisive, whatever the keys say. Q70 is the clean case: it is arithmetic.
RECALL — history, polity, current affairs, defence exercises. Defer to the
keys where they AGREE. Where they SPLIT and our own pass was LOW, the row
is not decidable from anything in this repo: both such rows (143, 144) were
left unresolved and then closed by the maintainer on external knowledge.
CALIBRATION — and the first published figure for this paper was MISLABELLED.
An earlier version of this file printed HIGH 121/127, MED 12/19, LOW 1/4 and
called it "measured against Centurion". Those are the DREAMERS figures. The
MED band differs a lot between the two keys, so the mislabel mattered:
our blind pass vs DREAMERS    HIGH 121/127 95.3%  MED 12/19 63.2%  LOW 1/4 25.0%

our blind pass vs ADJUDICATED HIGH 127/127  100%  MED 16/19 84.2%  LOW 1/4 25.0%
READ THE ADJUDICATED ROW WITH CARE — IT IS PARTLY CIRCULAR. The adjudicator
used our derivation and its reasoning as evidence, so a row resolved in our
favour scores our band as correct. HIGH reaching 127/127 therefore means every
HIGH row was adjudicated to our answer, which is a statement about the
adjudication as much as about the pass. The least circular number is the one
against CENTURION, which never saw our reasoning: HIGH 96.1%. What is NOT
circular either way is that all 6 rows whose stored answer changes are MED or

Against the same adjudicated answers: Centurion 145/150 (96.7%), OURS 144/150

keepOurs.class: SELF-REFUTING — and we depart from BOTH keys here
keepOurs.why: THE ONE ROW WHERE WE OVERRIDE A UNANIMOUS EXTERNAL VERDICT, so it is stated plainly. The stem asks which group of LANDLOCKED states borders Madhya Pradesh. MP's five neighbours are Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Maharashtra and Gujarat — and Maharashtra and Gujarat both have a coastline. Option A is all five, i.e. it answers 'which states border MP' and drops the stem's own qualifier. The option set is built to test exactly that qualifier: A ignores 'landlocked', B and C wrongly add Jharkhand (which does NOT border MP, Chhattisgarh separates them), D is the three landlocked ones. Two keys agreeing on A is consistent with two key-setters making the same highly available mistake — the correlated-error limit this project documents elsewhere. No amount of agreement makes Gujarat landlocked. Worth a human sanity-check precisely because it is unanimous against us. THIRD SOURCE NOW ALSO SAYS A, AND WE STILL HOLD D — because unlike the two keys it SHOWED ITS WORKING, and the working contains the mistake outright: it states "Madhya Pradesh shares its boundary with 5 landlocked states" and lists Maharashtra and Gujarat among them. Maharashtra has roughly 720 km of Arabian Sea coastline and Gujarat has the longest coastline of any Indian state, about 1,600 km. That sentence is false, and it is the whole basis for choosing A. Its process is visible too: it first answered C, then self-corrected to A on noticing that Jharkhand does not border MP, and never at any point tested the word "landlocked". So three sources now give A by what is demonstrably the same mechanism — reading the stem as "which states border MP" — which is the correlated-error hypothesis this row was flagged under, now with direct evidence rather than inference. Agreement across sources is not independence when the sources share a failure mode. If the maintainer prefers to ship A as the examiner-intended answer, that is a legitimate call, but it should be recorded as preserving a defective key rather than as a correction.

keepOurs.why: Re-derived rather than voted on. 252-250 = 2 g of steam condensed. Heat absorbed by the original water = 250 x 1 x (25-20) = 1250 Cal. Heat released = latent heat of condensation plus the cooling of that condensate from 100 to 25 = 2L + 2 x 1 x 75. Balancing, 2L = 1100 and L = 550 Cal/g, which is option C. No self-consistent reading of the stem returns Centurion's 560. A calculation is not a matter for majority vote.

Statement III is the false one and Centurion's 'all three' requires it to be true. NCERT Class 11 Physical Geography has the wind blowing PARALLEL to the isobars once the pressure-gradient and Coriolis forces balance; III asserts the opposite. I and II are both near-verbatim from the same chapter, including II's 'directly proportional to the angle of latitude', which is the book's own wording.

The stem asks which statements are NOT correct. II is false (soapstone is talc, the softest mineral on the Mohs scale, so granite is harder, not softer) and IV is false (foliation is a METAMORPHIC feature, not a sedimentary one), giving II and IV = C. Centurion's B would require rocks not to be aggregates of minerals and gabbro not to be black, both of which the same chapter states outright.

All three statements are items from the standard list of functions of political parties. Centurion's B excludes I — that in most democracies elections are fought mainly among party candidates — which is the first function the chapter lists.

flippedToOurs.why: REVERSED. Pair II is the textbook exclamatory transformation and is correct. Pair I keeps 'here' where reported speech shifts it to 'there', so it is not correctly stated — giving 'II only'. The first pass deferred on the explicit reasoning that 'the key is the only external signal' for a question of convention. That premise is now false: there are two signals, they disagree, and the one agreeing with the mechanical rule also agrees with our derivation. REVERSED, and recorded as genuinely contested. C is false (a uniform massive rope has tension varying along its length) and D is false (the heavier side descends, so the centre of mass accelerates), so the answer is A or B and the two differ only in how 'same acceleration' is read. Under a scalar reading the inextensibility constraint gives every point the same magnitude of acceleration, which is A and is the standard result taught at this level; under a strict vector reading the two sides accelerate in opposite directions, which is B. The first pass asserted that B was 'plainly what the item is testing' — an assertion, not evidence. Against it: our blind pass derived A and named B as the runner-up under exactly the vector reading, the second key says A, and a vector subtlety is out of character for a paper pitched at this level, where the distinctive physics is that tension is NOT uniform. A rigorous reading still favours B, so this is the row in the set most worth a second opinion. SETTLED: a third independent source reaches A on exactly the inextensible-rope constraint (same speed and same MAGNITUDE of acceleration at every point) and rejects C on the same ground we did, that a massive rope cannot have uniform tension. The contested flag is retired. The vector caveat is kept on record rather than deleted: over a pulley the two sides accelerate in opposite DIRECTIONS, so a strict vector reading of "same acceleration" still favours B, and a student who argues that is not confused. Three sources and the level of the paper settle it as A.

VERDICT UNCHANGED (A), now corroborated by a third source — but the tension is recorded in full because it is real and a student may raise it. The stem is scoped: "Consider the following statements in relation to respiration IN ANIMALS". Under that scope III ("carbon dioxide is released only in aerobic respiration") is TRUE, because animal anaerobic respiration gives lactic acid and no CO2 — which yields our C. All three external sources instead evaluate III as a general claim about respiration, where yeast fermentation releases CO2 and III is false, yielding A. The third source makes this explicit, calling III "incorrect AS A GENERAL STATEMENT" while conceding in the next line that in animals the product is lactic acid, not CO2 — i.e. it answers against a scope the stem does not use. We defer to A because it is what three independent sources give and what the examiner evidently intended, NOT because the scope argument is wrong. Our deriver marked this MED and named the tension in advance.

acceptKeys.class: RECALL — OUR ANSWER WAS WRONG; Centurion alone was right
acceptKeys.settledBy: maintainer, 2026-09-14, citing reporting on the 2026 Goldman Environmental Prize
acceptKeys.why: SETTLED AS D (II and III). Statement I is false (the prize is annual) and II is true — six winners, one per region, with Borim Kim of South Korea representing Asia. III is TRUE: all six 2026 winners were women, reported as the first time this has happened in the prize’s history. Accepted on named, checkable sources plus a falsifiable specific, and independently corroborated by Centurion; NOT independently verified here. This is a genuine correction to our answer, and the way our pass failed is the useful part: the deriver reasoned from a BASE RATE — that an all-women slate is unlikely — and the sources say 2026 is the first year it ever happened. A base-rate argument against an unprecedented event is correct every year until the year it is not, and it carries no signal about which year that is. The deriver was right to mark this LOW and right to name III as the hinge; the error was answering at all rather than declining.
